query: For nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near-equal atomic ratios and initially crystallized as a solid solution, what governs whether structural and chemical stability is maintained across catalytic and thermoelectric operating ranges of 473–1923 K? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled comparison, predict observations relative to the initial baseline, define the conditions under which the prediction should hold, identify supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The degree of local lattice distortion, emerging from both static bond length variations (due to atomic radii mismatches) and local chemical fluctuations (notably electronegativity differences), governs whether equimolar multi-metal nanoparticles maintain a stable single-phase solid solution under catalytic and thermoelectric operations from 473 K to 1923 K.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles composed of five or more metals in equal or near‐equal atomic ratios, initially crystallized as a homogeneous solid solution.
generation.intervention: Alter the nanoparticle composition by substituting one or more elements to systematically vary the magnitude of atomic radii and electronegativity differences while preserving overall equimolar proportions.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted from 473 K to 1923 K under catalytic and thermoelectric operating conditions in inert or reducing atmospheres to minimize oxidation effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions generated by the combined effects of atomic size mismatch and chemical fluctuation.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced lattice distortion elevates an effective temperature that raises the energetic barrier for phase separation or ordering. This suppression of detrimental atomic rearrangements preserves the single-phase solid solution over a broad temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoparticles engineered with greater lattice distortion (via larger atomic radii and stronger electronegativity contrasts) will retain their single-phase structure and stable catalytic/thermoelectric properties at temperatures up to 1923 K, while those with minimal distortion will be more prone to phase segregation or ordering at lower temperatures.
generation.baseline: The original equimolar nanoparticles exhibiting moderate, inherent lattice distortions that afford some stability at moderate temperatures.
generation.boundary: This prediction holds provided that nanoparticle size effects, surface oxidation, and non-equilibrium conditions do not dominate the structural behavior, and the measured properties reflect intrinsic material responses rather than extrinsic influences.
generation.uncertainty: The impact of nanoscale effects (e.g., surface-to-volume ratio and defect densities) on the effective combination of static and dynamic lattice distortions is not fully understood and may modify the stabilization mechanism compared to bulk materials.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of equimolar nanoparticles: one set with intentionally increased lattice distortion (by choosing elements with larger disparities in atomic radii and electronegativity) and a control set with reduced lattice distortion. Subject both sets to identical catalytic and thermoelectric testing across 473 K to 1923 K.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to monitor phase stability
Atomic-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) to assess local lattice distortions
Catalytic performance metrics and thermoelectric property measurements (e.g., electrical conductivity and Seebeck coefficient) over the temperature range
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the control set (with lower lattice distortion) maintains similar or superior structural and chemical stability, along with catalytic and thermoelectric properties, relative to the high-distortion set across the entire temperature range, the hypothesis would be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractLattice distortions are intrinsic features of all solid solution alloys associated with varying atomic radii; this phenomenon facilitates the formation of single-phase solid solutions. Using high-entropy alloys (HEAs), as an example, we investigate the influence of variations in inter-atomic separations for stabilizing and controlling their structural, mechanical, and thermodynamic properties. This is done through a combination of statistical mechanics analysis and molecular dynamics simulations on simplified 2D systems, as well as a 3D crystals with harmonic and anharmonic inter-atomic bonds with varying natural inter-atomic separations. We demonstrate that the impact of this inter-atomic length disorder (representing static lattice distortion) and temperature fluctuations (representing dynamic lattice distortion) on fundamental and universal thermodynamic, structural, and elastic characteristics are similar and can be unified through effective temperature; i.e. a scaling law for HEAs that establishes a relationship between these factors. ## Abstract
In high-entropy materials, local chemical fluctuation from multiple elements inhabiting the same crystallographic site plays a crucial role in their unique properties. Using atomic-resolution chemical mapping, we identified the respective contributions of different element characteristics on the local chemical fluctuation of high-entropy structures in thermoelectric materials. Electronegativity and mass had a comparable influence on the fluctuations of constituent elements, while the radius made a slight contribution. The local chemical fluctuation was further tailored by selecting specific elements to induce large lattice distortion and strong strain fluctuation to lower lattice thermal conductivity independent of increased entropy. The chemical bond fluctuation induced by the electronegativity difference had a noticeable contribution to the composition-dependent lattice thermal conductivity in addition to the known fluctuations of mass and strain field. Our findings provide a fundamental principle for tuning local chemical fluctuation and lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy thermoelectric materials.
